title: Iran's Economy Buckles Under US War Pressure as Inflation Hits 89% and Jobs Vanish
excerpt: With oil revenues squeezed by a renewed US blockade and consumer prices spiraling, ordinary Iranians are buying groceries on credit while the regime debates whether to hold the Strait of Hormuz or seek a deal.
body:
• Iran's consumer inflation reached 88.6% year-over-year in June, with egg prices in Tehran surging 40% in just days
  • The IMF projects Iran's GDP will shrink 5.4% this year as the US blockade chokes oil revenue — the regime's main source of hard currency
  • Economists estimate 2 to 3 million jobs could be lost as factories close and trade corridors remain disrupted
  • A deepening split between regime pragmatists and hard-liners over control of the Strait of Hormuz complicates any path to relief

Iran's wartime economy is entering a phase that economists describe as a self-reinforcing crisis, where recession and inflation feed off each other with no clear exit in sight.

Consumer prices in June were up 88.6% from a year earlier, according to official Iranian statistics. In Tehran, the price of a tray of eggs shot up 40% in just the first few days of July — to the equivalent of $3.30 — according to Iran's Fars news agency. Families are buying rice, meat and pasta on credit through a government program. Others are eliminating meat from meals and purchasing staples one item at a time as wages lose value.

The Blockade Bites Again

The collapse of a June deal between Washington and Tehran has reversed the brief economic relief Iran had secured. President Trump's decision to reimpose the naval blockade and revoke Iran's right to sell oil has cut off the regime's primary source of hard currency.

https://x.com/torax_fi/status/2089003511522484542

In the four weeks after the June agreement, Iran shipped nearly 70 million barrels of oil worth an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion, according to data provider Kpler. But that window has closed.

"The impact of the blockade will be similar to the U.S. blockade in April. Production will drop, inventories will fill up."

— Homayoun Falakshahi, Head of Crude Oil Analysis, Kpler

Some analysts estimate that a blockade lasting four to five months could reduce Iran's oil revenues to close to zero. When oil exports decline, fewer dollars enter the economy, making imported food, medicine and industrial components more expensive. Manufacturers facing higher costs and shortages then cut production and jobs.

A Survival Economy Under Strain

The International Monetary Fund projects Iran's gross domestic product will shrink by 5.4% this year — a forecast made before the latest round of fighting intensified.

Hadi Kahalzadeh, an economist and former official in Iran's Social Security Organization, estimates the war could cost Iran 2 million to 3 million jobs. According to his calculations, only the top 3% of Iranian households can now afford the full food basket recommended by health officials.

"The renewed blockade would intensify this hardship and feed into further currency depreciation, inflation, shortages, factory closures and employment losses. Perhaps the most damaging economic factor is the absence of a credible horizon for stabilization."

— Hadi Kahalzadeh, Economist

A 38-year-old university arts professor in Tehran told the Wall Street Journal that prices for supplies such as brushes, paints and canvases had doubled since March. Her biggest fear, she said, is for her sick child who depends on an oxygen machine powered by unreliable electricity.

Regime Split Clouds Any Path Forward

An Iranian diplomat described a deepening fracture within the regime between pragmatists who worry the blockade will worsen the ailing economy and hard-liners who want to aggressively assert control of the Strait of Hormuz as leverage over the United States.

"Iran is prepared to pay a very, very high cost, including the continued blockade by the American side, in order to retain and sustain this control over the Strait of Hormuz going forward," said Ellie Geranmayeh, an Iran expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations. "In the Iranian mentality, it's just about surviving another day, and then another day."

Iran's Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad insisted Tuesday that Iran has deployed systems for years to skirt US sanctions. But the April blockade showed how quickly those workarounds can collapse — Iranian crude exports fell sharply before the temporary agreement allowed shipments to resume in June.

What Comes Next

The risk, analysts say, is an increasingly damaging stalemate: Washington inflicts severe economic pain that fails to translate quickly into Iranian concessions over the strait, while Tehran presides over a poorer and more precarious society. The renewed pressure may push the regime back to negotiations, but it could also strengthen hard-liners who view any concession as an existential threat. For ordinary Iranians, the calculation is simpler — the financial strain may well outlast the conflict itself.
